planting.note: Set dormant one-year crowns into trenches 6-8 inches deep as soon as soil is workable in spring, then gradually backfill as spears emerge.

directions: Jersey King is one of the Rutgers all-male hybrid asparagus lines bred for resistance to Fusarium crown rot and asparagus rust while eliminating the volunteer seedlings that female plants produce. It sends up thick, uniform, deep-green spears with tightly closed tips over a long spring harvest window. Because energy is not diverted into seed production, established beds tend to build vigor faster than open-pollinated types like Mary Washington. Give plants a full season to establish before taking any harvest, and top-dress with compost each fall to sustain crown health for decades.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

planting.note: Plant crowns in raised ridges or mounded soil so spears can be earthed up for blanching if white asparagus is desired.

directions: Gijnlim is a Dutch all-male hybrid developed for the European white and green asparagus trade, prized for spearing very early in spring and producing an unusually concentrated first flush of thick, straight spears. Growers who mound soil over the crowns get pale, tender spears for traditional white asparagus, while unmounded beds yield classic green spears just as reliably. Its early emergence means it can beat frost-sensitive varieties to market by a week or more in cool climates. Established beds reward deep, fertile, well-drained soil and a thick mulch layer to suppress weeds between rows.

planting.note: Enrich the bed with well-rotted manure before planting one-year crowns, since this old heirloom rewards deep, rich soil.

directions: Brock's Imperial is an old open-pollinated English heirloom asparagus valued for producing exceptionally thick, well-flavored spears on vigorous, long-lived crowns. Because it is not an all-male hybrid, plants include both sexes, so expect some volunteer seedlings from the red berries that female plants set in late summer. Gardeners who favor traditional, seed-saveable strains over modern hybrids often choose it to keep an older lineage of asparagus in circulation. Allow a full two seasons of foliage growth before the first light harvest to build a strong root system.

planting.note: Sow seed directly or start indoors in early spring; unlike most rhubarb it can be lightly cropped in its first year.

directions: Glaskin's Perpetual is a seed-grown heirloom rhubarb bred to bolt (flower) far less readily than most seed strains, so stalk production stays steady all season instead of stalling after the plant runs to seed. Its notably low oxalic acid content lets gardeners take a light first-year harvest, a rarity among rhubarbs that normally need a full year or two to establish before cropping. Stalks are medium-thick and pink-green rather than deep red, with a mild, less astringent flavor suited to lighter sweetening. It remains popular with gardeners who want a reliable, true-breeding rhubarb they can start cheaply from seed rather than buying divisions.

planting.note: Divide and plant dormant crowns in autumn or very early spring into deeply enriched soil, leaving the growing bud just below the surface.

directions: Hawke's Champagne is a classic English forcing rhubarb known for pushing up exceptionally early, slender pink-red stalks when crowns are covered with a forcing pot or brought into a dark shed in late winter. Left unforced it still crops earlier than most maincrop varieties, making it a favorite for gardeners chasing the first rhubarb of the year. Its slender stalks are sweeter and less fibrous than the stalks of many later, thicker-stemmed cultivars, needing less added sugar in cooking. Rest forced crowns for a full season afterward so they can rebuild reserves before forcing again.

planting.note: Plant dormant crowns in autumn or early spring in a sunny, well-drained bed enriched with aged manure or compost.

directions: Stockbridge Arrow is a modern British-bred maincrop rhubarb selected for long, straight, uniformly deep-red stalks and strong disease resistance, and it has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. It holds its color and firm texture well into midsummer rather than fading to green like many older varieties, which makes it popular with market growers as well as home gardeners. Vigorous, disease-resistant crowns establish quickly and produce heavy yields once mature. Divide congested clumps every four to six years in dormancy to keep stalk quality high.
